Still, she did hear through the news media about the killing by another member of FARC of Ivan Rios, a member of the group's central high command. "We suffered a very strong blow," she said. She acknowledged that news led her to worry about the possibility that one of her fellow guerrillas might consider doing the same thing to her. "A person has a lot of combatants alongside, but you don't know what each one is thinking," she said. Asked about news reports of guerrilla operations she may have participated in, Karina admitted to nothing. "They accuse me of a lot of things I wasn't part of," she said. But Miguel Antonio Paez told CNN en Espanol that he remembers well the woman who, with a band of guerrillas, stopped the bus he was on in 2004 in northwest Colombia, ordered him and the other passengers off and the bus be burned. "The commander of that guerrilla group -- a dark-haired woman, tall, with one eye missing -- called herself Karina," he said. "She ordered me tied up. Here, I have the marks from the wires, and there, while I was tied up, she lopped off my penis and testicles and I remained castrated for all my life." Asked specifically about the killing of the father of President Alvaro Uribe in 1983, she said she did not know who carried out the act, and added, "I don't have my hands stained in that deed." She said that with her surrender have come new fears about possible retribution from FARC loyalists, who consider her a traitor. Wearing a red sweatshirt and what appeared to be a diamond earring in her left ear, she said she once believed the FARC would rule Colombia. "I once dreamed of that," she said. Gen. Mario Montoya, chief of the army, said two Colombian air force helicopters were sent Sunday to pick up Karina and her companion, who had given authorities their general location. "With this, we have given a confounding strike to the FARC structure," particularly to Front 47, which at this point is practically dismantled," he said. Since the killing of Rios, 45 members of the group have laid down their arms and accepted a government plan for reinstallation into society, he said. "We want to send a message to all members of FARC who persist in the mountains," he said. "To tell them, what Karina has done is the road all the members of FARC should go down. If they don't, we are going to continue combating them. Today, more than ever, I invite them to lay down their arms, take the plan. We don't want them dead. We want them alive."

After spending 24 years within the ranks of the organization, Karina made the dramatic decision to lay down her arms and surrender to Colombian authorities.

Speaking to reporters gathered in the capital city of Bogota, Karina delivered a message that stood in stark contrast to the violent path she had followed for most of her adult life. Her words carried particular weight coming from someone who had once been a committed and battle-hardened fighter for the rebel cause.

When explaining the reasoning behind her defection, Karina pointed directly to the relentless military pressure that government forces had brought to bear against the FARC. Beyond simply surrendering herself, Karina went a step further by publicly calling on her fellow rebels to follow her example and abandon the armed struggle. This appeal, made by such a prominent figure, represented a significant symbolic and strategic blow to the FARC's cohesion and morale.

Her defection came at a particularly vulnerable moment for the guerrilla group, which was grappling with serious internal turmoil. The organization had been shaken by the killing of a high command member at the hands of another rebel—a shocking act of internal violence that underscored the fractures and mistrust spreading through the FARC's leadership. Karina herself admitted to harboring fears that she might meet a similar fate, targeted and eliminated from within the very organization to which she had devoted more than two decades of her life. # FARC Commander "Karina" Surrenders to Colombian Authorities

**One of the guerrilla group's most feared female leaders lays down arms**

BOGOTA, Colombia — Nelly Ávila Moreno, the notorious FARC commander known by her nom de guerre "Karina," surrendered to Colombian authorities, marking a significant blow to the leftist rebel group that has waged war against the government for decades.

Karina, who commanded the FARC's 47th Front and was one of the few women to reach a position of significant power within the guerrilla organization, turned herself in along with a companion after years as one of the country's most wanted insurgents.

## A Feared Commander Speaks

Appearing at a news conference, the guerrilla leader — recognizable by the eye she lost in combat years ago — spoke about her decision to abandon the armed struggle.

"I got tired of the war," Karina told reporters. "I invite my compañeros to leave the guerrilla life. The war is not worth it."

She described the mounting pressure that led to her decision, citing relentless military operations that had decimated her ranks and left her isolated in the jungle.

"I felt the ground disappearing beneath my feet," she said. "The military operations gave us no rest. We were being hunted constantly."

Karina, who was blamed for numerous kidnappings, killings, and attacks during her time with the FARC, appeared to express contrition for her role in the conflict.

"I ask forgiveness from the people of Colombia," she said.

## Military Officials React

Colombian military officials hailed the surrender as evidence that their intensified campaign against the FARC was working.

Then-Defense Minister Juan Manuel Santos called the surrender a major achievement, saying it demonstrated the growing weakness within the rebel ranks.

"This is a clear sign that the FARC is crumbling," a senior military official said. "When commanders of Karina's stature choose to surrender, it sends a powerful message to the rank and file."

Military leaders emphasized that pressure from government forces had made continued resistance untenable for many guerrilla fighters.

"Our strategy of sustained pressure is yielding results," an army spokesman said. "We continue to offer demobilization to those who wish to return to civilian life."

## A Symbolic Blow

Karina's surrender was widely viewed as both a strategic and symbolic victory for the Colombian government. As one of the FARC's most prominent female commanders, her defection was seen as a demoralizing development for the organization.

Government officials used the occasion to renew their appeals to remaining guerrilla fighters to abandon the decades-long conflict, which has claimed thousands of lives and displaced millions of Colombians.

The surrender came amid a period of intensified military operations against the FARC that had resulted in the deaths and captures of several high-ranking rebel leaders.

---

*This article is presented in the style of a news report. For the most current information about Colombia and the FARC peace process, please consult up-to-date news sources.*

# Former FARC Commander Lays Down Arms, Speaks of Reconciliation and Reckoning

*A high-profile defection reopens questions about accountability, forgiveness, and the fragile architecture of Colombia's peace*

---

**BOGOTÁ, Colombia** — For more than two decades, the woman known within guerrilla ranks as "Comandante Marisol" moved through the dense jungles of Colombia's southern departments, rising from a teenage recruit to a mid-level commander in one of the hemisphere's oldest insurgencies. This week, in a heavily secured government facility on the outskirts of the capital, she sat across from a small group of journalists and declared that her war was over.

"I gave my youth to a revolution I believed would liberate the poor," she said, her voice steady but her hands folded tightly on the table. "I am no longer certain that anything we did brought liberation. What I know is that it brought graves."

Her defection—confirmed by officials from the Office of the High Commissioner for Peace—marks one of the most significant departures from the dissident factions that rejected the landmark 2016 accord between the Colombian government and the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia, or FARC. That agreement formally ended a conflict that killed at least 220,000 people and displaced millions over more than half a century.

## A Life Inside the Insurgency

Marisol, whose legal identity the government has withheld pending her participation in transitional justice proceedings, says she was recruited at 15 from a rural hamlet in Caquetá, a region where the state's presence has historically been thin and the economy long distorted by coca cultivation.

"There was no school after a certain age. There was no clinic. There were the guerrillas, and they offered a rifle and a purpose," she recalled. "When you are young and angry and hungry, that is a powerful thing."

She rose through the ranks during the height of the conflict in the early 2000s, eventually commanding a unit responsible for logistics, extortion collection, and, according to a preliminary government dossier, participation in kidnappings that were a hallmark of FARC operations during that period.

Marisol did not dispute the broad outlines of that record.

"I will not stand here and tell you my hands are clean," she said. "That would be an insult to the people who suffered. I answered for orders. I gave orders. Both of those are true."

When the 2016 accord was signed, she was among those who initially demobilized. But like an estimated several thousand fighters, she grew disillusioned with what she described as the government's failure to deliver on promised rural development and security guarantees, and she rejoined an armed dissident structure.

"They told us the peace would bring roads, titles to our land, protection," she said. "Instead our comrades who laid down their weapons were being killed, one by one. So some of us picked the rifle back up. I tell you honestly: it was a mistake. I traded one betrayal for another."

## The Decision to Leave

Marisol says her final break came after a series of internal disputes over the dissident factions' deepening entanglement with drug trafficking networks—a transformation that she argues stripped the movement of whatever ideological legitimacy it once claimed.

"It stopped being about the campesino," she said. "It became about the cargo. When you are protecting shipments instead of people, you are no longer a revolutionary. You are a businessman with a gun."

Government officials confirmed she made contact through an intermediary several months ago and has since provided intelligence, though they declined to specify its nature. Her cooperation, they said, will be weighed by the Special Jurisdiction for Peace (JEP), the tribunal established under the 2016 accord to adjudicate crimes committed during the conflict.

The JEP offers reduced, non-carceral sanctions to those who confess fully and contribute to truth and reparations—a controversial mechanism that critics say lets perpetrators avoid prison, but that supporters argue was essential to ending the war at all.

"I am prepared to tell the truth," Marisol said. "Not for leniency. For the families. They have a right to know where the bodies are. I know where some of them are."

## A Victim Remembers

For those who lived through the guerrillas' campaigns, statements of contrition arrive freighted with a complicated grief.

Esperanza Ruiz, 58, lost her husband in a 2003 kidnapping in the department of Meta. He was a small landowner, seized for a ransom the family spent three years and everything they owned trying to pay. His body was never recovered.

Reached by telephone, Ruiz said she had followed news of the defection with a mixture of hope and exhaustion.

"They always speak of peace now," she said. "For twenty years I have heard them speak of peace. But my children grew up without their father. There is no accord that gives me back what was taken."

Yet Ruiz stopped short of dismissing the value of a commander's confession.

"If this woman knows where the disappeared are, then let her speak. Let her speak every name she remembers," she said. "I do not need her to weep for cameras. I need her to tell a mother where her son is buried. That is the only apology that means anything."

Asked whether she could forgive, Ruiz was quiet for a long moment.

"Forgiveness is not a gift I owe them," she said finally. "But truth—truth I will accept. Truth is the beginning."

When Marisol was told of Ruiz's words, she lowered her eyes.

"She is right to demand it," she said. "I do not ask to be forgiven. I ask only to be useful to the truth. That is the last order I will follow."

## The Fragile Peace

Marisol's defection unfolds against a broader struggle to consolidate a peace that remains, eight years on, deeply incomplete. Human rights organizations have documented the killings of hundreds of demobilized ex-combatants and social leaders since the accord's signing. Dissident factions and other armed groups continue to contest territory across rural Colombia, financed largely by the drug trade and illegal mining.

Analysts caution that individual defections, however symbolically potent, do not by themselves reverse those dynamics.

"A single commander leaving is meaningful, but it is not a strategy," said a Bogotá-based conflict researcher who has studied the demobilization process. "The state has to demonstrate that laying down arms leads to a viable, protected life. As long as ex-combatants are being murdered, the incentive structure works against peace."

Government officials framed Marisol's departure as evidence that the door remains open to those willing to leave the armed groups—part of the current administration's broader "total peace" initiative seeking negotiated settlements with remaining factions.

Whether that framing holds may depend on cases exactly like this one: whether a woman who spent her life in the jungle can translate her stated remorse into the specific, verifiable truths that victims like Esperanza Ruiz are still waiting to hear.

## An Uncertain Reckoning

As the interview drew to a close, Marisol was asked what she would say to the young people in regions like the one where she was recruited—places where, she conceded, the same conditions that led her to the guerrillas still persist.

"I would tell them the rifle is a lie," she said. "It promises you dignity and it delivers you a grave, or it makes you the one who digs them. I believed the lie for most of my life. I am telling the truth now because it is the only thing I have left to give."

She will remain in state custody as her case proceeds through the transitional justice system—a process expected to take years, and one that will test whether Colombia's hard-won and still-fragile peace can hold space for both accountability and reconciliation.

For Ruiz, the calculus is simpler, and far older than any accord.

"Let her talk," she said. "There are mothers still waiting. We have been waiting a very long time."

---

*Editor's note: Certain identifying details have been withheld at the request of Colombian authorities, citing ongoing legal proceedings and security concerns.*

**BOGOTÁ, Colombia** — One of Colombia's most-wanted female guerrilla commanders surrendered to military authorities on Tuesday, marking a significant blow to insurgent forces operating in the country's remote southern jungles, army officials said.

The commander, known by her nom de guerre "Comandante Esperanza," turned herself in at a military base in Caquetá province after more than 15 years with the rebel group, according to a statement from the Colombian Armed Forces.

At a press conference arranged by military officials, the former commander, dressed in civilian clothing and appearing composed, addressed reporters about her decision to abandon the armed struggle.

"I have spent half my life in these mountains, and I have seen too many young people die for a cause that has lost its way," she told journalists gathered at the base. "I want other women who are still out there to know that there is a path back. The war is over for me."

# Former FARC Commander Renounces Armed Struggle, Urges Dialogue Amid Controversy

## A High-Profile Departure from the Insurgency

In a development that has drawn attention across Colombia's ongoing peace landscape, a former commander of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) has publicly abandoned the armed insurgency, issuing a call for political dialogue over continued warfare. Her departure marks another chapter in the long and complicated dissolution of what was once Latin America's oldest and most powerful guerrilla movement.

Speaking to reporters, the former commander framed her decision as a repudiation of the path of violence. "The time for weapons has passed," she said, according to statements circulated to media. "Colombia needs voices willing to build peace through conversation, not bullets. I am choosing that path."

## From Combatant to Advocate for Dialogue

The commander, who spent years within the FARC's ranks and rose to a position of authority, described a gradual disillusionment with the armed struggle. She pointed to the toll the decades-long conflict has taken on rural communities, combatants, and civilians alike.

Her appeal for dialogue echoes the framework established by the historic 2016 peace accord between the Colombian government and the FARC, which formally ended more than half a century of conflict and led to the demobilization of thousands of fighters. That agreement transformed the bulk of the FARC into a legal political party, though dissident factions rejected the deal and continued to operate.

## Accusations and Legal Questions

The commander's exit has not been without controversy. Authorities and critics have leveled a range of accusations against her, tied to activities allegedly carried out during her time with the insurgency. These reportedly include involvement in violent actions, recruitment, and participation in the group's broader operations against state forces and civilians.

Such allegations place her in a complicated position under Colombia's transitional justice system, known as the Special Jurisdiction for Peace (JEP). That mechanism was designed to weigh accountability against reconciliation, offering reduced sentences to former combatants who confess to their roles, tell the truth to victims, and commit to reparations. Those who fail to cooperate face the prospect of conventional prosecution and harsher penalties.

Her call for dialogue, therefore, carries legal weight as much as symbolic significance—her cooperation could influence how her case is ultimately handled.

## Official Comments on the FARC's Dismantling

Government officials have pointed to defections and demobilizations as evidence of the continued erosion of armed groups. Security officials have characterized the departure as a further sign that the original FARC structure has been effectively dismantled, with remaining armed activity now concentrated among dissident cells and other criminal or insurgent organizations.

"The FARC as it once existed no longer functions as a unified military force," officials have suggested in describing the current security environment. Authorities emphasize ongoing efforts to encourage remaining fighters to lay down arms and enter the peace process, while continuing military and police operations against groups that reject dialogue.

Analysts caution, however, that the disappearance of the original FARC has not brought an end to violence in Colombia. Dissident factions, the National Liberation Army (ELN), and various armed groups continue to compete for territory, drug trafficking routes, and illegal mining revenues—particularly in remote regions where the state's presence remains limited.

## The Broader Peace Landscape

The commander's decision unfolds against the backdrop of Colombia's broader "total peace" ambitions, which have sought to negotiate with multiple armed actors simultaneously. Progress has been uneven, marked by ceasefires, breakdowns, and renewed talks.

For victims of the conflict, high-profile defections raise difficult questions about justice, truth, and reconciliation. Victims' advocates stress that any calls for dialogue must be accompanied by genuine accountability and meaningful reparations, not merely symbolic gestures.

As Colombia continues to navigate the long aftermath of its armed conflict, the former commander's renunciation of violence—and the accusations that shadow it—illustrates the enduring tensions between the imperatives of peace and the demands of justice.
